title: "How Iterators Work"

# How Iterators Work

An iterator is a value with a `next` method that returns `Some(item)` or `None`. Everything else in this part is a loop around that method, or a type that delays the loop.

## The concept

```rust
pub trait Iterator {
    type Item;
    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<Self::Item>;
}
```

`next` takes `&mut self`, so pulling an item changes the iterator. The sequence itself may be borrowed (`iter` yields `&T`), mutably borrowed (`iter_mut` yields `&mut T`), or owned (`into_iter` yields `T` and consumes the collection).

`for` loops, `collect`, and `sum` are consumers. `map` and `filter` are adaptors: they return a new iterator and call the inner `next` only when they are themselves pulled.

## Recipe 1 — Iterating over a Vec without cloning

Borrow the vector. Each item is a reference, so `String` stays where it is.

```rust
fn main() {
    let names = vec![
        String::from("ada"),
        String::from("linus"),
        String::from("grace"),
    ];

    let mut labels = Vec::new();
    for name in &names {
        labels.push(name.to_uppercase());
    }

    assert_eq!(names.len(), 3);
    assert_eq!(labels, ["ADA", "LINUS", "GRACE"]);
}
```

`for name in &names` is the same sequence as `names.iter()`. `name` has type `&String`. Cloning would be `names.clone()` or `name.clone()` inside the loop, and neither is required to read the names.

If the loop must change the strings in place, borrow mutably:

```rust
fn main() {
    let mut names = vec![String::from("ada"), String::from("linus")];
    for name in &mut names {
        name.push_str("!");
    }
    assert_eq!(names, ["ada!", "linus!"]);
}
```

## Recipe 2 — Building an infinite iterator with next()

A counter that never returns `None` is still a valid iterator. The caller decides when to stop.

```rust
struct CountFrom {
    n: u32,
}

impl Iterator for CountFrom {
    type Item = u32;

    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<Self::Item> {
        let current = self.n;
        self.n += 1;
        Some(current)
    }
}

fn main() {
    let mut ids = CountFrom { n: 10 };
    assert_eq!(ids.next(), Some(10));
    assert_eq!(ids.next(), Some(11));

    let first_three: Vec<_> = CountFrom { n: 0 }.take(3).collect();
    assert_eq!(first_three, [0, 1, 2]);
}
```

`take(3)` is what makes the infinite iterator finite. Without a consumer that stops, `collect` on `CountFrom` would not return.

`std::iter::from_fn` is the same idea without a named type:

```rust
fn main() {
    let mut n = 0u32;
    let mut ids = std::iter::from_fn(move || {
        let current = n;
        n += 1;
        Some(current)
    });
    assert_eq!(ids.next(), Some(0));
    assert_eq!(ids.next(), Some(1));
}
```

The closure is `FnMut`. `move` captures `n` so the iterator owns its state.

## Recipe 3 — Understanding why .map() alone does nothing

`map` stores the closure. It does not call it.

```rust
fn main() {
    use std::cell::Cell;

    let calls = Cell::new(0);
    let readings = [1, 2, 3, 4];
    let scaled = readings.iter().map(|n| {
        calls.set(calls.get() + 1);
        n * 10
    });

    assert_eq!(calls.get(), 0);

    let out: Vec<_> = scaled.collect();
    assert_eq!(out, [10, 20, 30, 40]);
    assert_eq!(calls.get(), 4);
}
```

`Cell` is only here so the closure can count calls without claiming `&mut` from `main` while `readings` is borrowed. The point is the count: it stays `0` until `collect` pulls every item.

Drop the iterator without consuming it and the closure never runs:

```rust
fn main() {
    use std::cell::Cell;

    let calls = Cell::new(0);
    let _scaled = [1, 2, 3].iter().map(|n| {
        calls.set(calls.get() + 1);
        n * 10
    });
    assert_eq!(calls.get(), 0);
}
```

That is why a pipeline that "should have printed" and didn't is usually missing `collect`, `for`, `sum`, or another consumer.
